card.hook: Picture a bold red-and-white lighthouse perched at the end of a cliff, with nothing behind it but sea and sky. That's Cape Spartel, and the tower is the star.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 2 km south-west of the subject, and face north-east. Look along the headland and you'll spot the red-and-white tower.
card.zoom: Try zoom 2x if your phone has it, so the tower stands out against the sea and sky. On 1x the tower looks small, which can actually show off the scale. Switch to 0.5x for the whole headland and lots of sky.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the tower, then slide the brightness down a little so the white parts and the sky keep their detail.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day, and Spain may even show across the strait. Check on your screen where the sun is first, so it isn't shining straight into your phone as you look at the tower.
card.selfie_here: Head for the wooden sign where the Atlantic meets the Mediterranean, about 500 m south of the lighthouse along the main road (you can walk there from the lighthouse). Stand in front of it with the Atlantic on your left and the Mediterranean on your right, use the front camera, and try 0.5x so the sign fits behind you.
card.ask_someone: On the lighthouse grounds, ask a passer-by to snap you standing in front of the tower, so the lighthouse is your backdrop.
card.rules_and_safety: It's windy and the rocks can be slippery, so keep a few paces back from any cliff edge. Take care with children on the main road between the lighthouse and the sign. The tower and museum may need a ticket or have restrictions, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines, put the tower on a vertical line and the horizon on a horizontal one, then leave a little empty space beside it. Take a few frames in case the wind makes you wobble.
card.good_to_know: Cape Spartel is the north-westernmost point of the African continent, about 300 metres above the sea. The lighthouse was built under Sultan Muhammad IV in 1864. The site was renovated in 2020-2021 and now has a maritime museum, a restaurant and a botanical garden.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 2 km south-west of the subject, and face north-east. Look along the headland and you'll spot the red-and-white tower.

selfie_spots.why: A travel guide calls this sign a top photo point, and the sea-meeting framing makes it a strong backdrop for a selfie.

card.hook: Here's the twist: the Kasbah Palace isn't in this photo at all. What you get is a white lane, an arched gateway and a neat slice of blue sea, and it's the classic Kasbah shot.
card.stand_here: Stand on Bab el Assa, in the lane beside the gate where it steps down toward the strait. Face down the lane, and the palace is a very short walk to the north-west behind the shot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the gateway, the white walls and the sea in one frame. Then try 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look, and 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the arch or a patch of sea.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the arch or lane edges on the outer lines so the walls lead the eye to the sea, then tap the bright sea and slide it a little darker so the white walls keep their detail.
card.best_time: Go late in the day, when the light turns warm, according to one guide. That's when the white walls look their friendliest.
card.selfie_here: Head to the edge of Place de la Kasbah, the square's highest point, and use the front camera at 0.5x with the port and the Strait of Gibraltar behind you. If you go into the first courtyard of Dar el Makhzen, the central fountain is a popular selfie spot, especially in morning light.
card.ask_someone: On Place de la Kasbah, in front of the palace's decorated main entrance, hand your phone to a passer-by and ask for one with the entrance behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The lane and the outside views are open public streets, but the museum inside is a separate matter, so check on site before you go in. Photos inside are generally fine without flash.
card.challenge: Turn on Live Photo and catch someone walking through the gateway, then pick your favourite frame.
card.good_to_know: The Kasbah Palace, also called Dar el Makhzen, was the old governor's residence. It was built in the early 18th century under Sultan Moulay Ismail, on the ruins of an English castle. It has been a museum since 1922 and reopened after a big renovation in 2016. Inside, two courtyards have decorated wooden ceilings and marble fountains.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Bab el Assa, in the lane beside the gate where it steps down toward the strait. Face down the lane, and the palace is a very short walk to the north-west behind the shot.

card.hook: Here's a fun one: in the middle of a narrow medina lane, a whole room stretches over your head like a bridge, with an eagle crest sitting above the archway. Most people walk under it without looking up, so don't be most people.
card.stand_here: Stand on Rue d'Amérique, approaching from the south, on the lane in front of the arched reception room. From the medina, the Legation lies to the east, about 5 minutes on foot. Face the arch and look up to fit in the crest.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the arch and the crest together. If the lane is too tight to get the whole archway in, tap 0.5x. For a close-up of the eagle crest, try zoom 2x.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the arch or crest, then drag the slider to make it a little darker so the bright sky above the lane doesn't wash out the stonework.
card.best_time: Early morning is the sweet spot: the lane is likely to be quieter and the light is softer. Skip the middle of the day, when the sky above the lane is very bright against the shaded walls.
card.selfie_here: Try Rue d'Amérique in front of the arched reception room, which is probably your best backdrop outside. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if you can, and let the arch and crest sit over your shoulder. Inside, the museum courtyard is also a good spot for photos.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Rue d'Amérique to the south, far enough back to take in the whole arched reception room, while you stand in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: The lane is narrow, so step aside for pedestrians and traffic before you stop to shoot. Inside, photography is generally allowed, but some areas are restricted, so ask the staff first.
card.challenge: Get the arch, the crest and the lane's leading lines in one shot, with the phone held perfectly level so the walls don't lean.
card.good_to_know: The sultan gave this building to the American government, and the legation was established in 1821. It served as a diplomatic post for about 140 years and is the only U.S. National Historic Landmark outside the United States. Today it's a museum, cultural centre and research library, with a set of rooms devoted to the writer and composer Paul Bowles.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Rue d'Amérique, approaching from the south, on the lane in front of the arched reception room. From the medina, the Legation lies to the east, about 5 minutes on foot. Face the arch and look up to fit in the crest.

card.hook: Picture a cliff-top cafe where the tables step down in whitewashed terraces and, on a clear day, Spain sits on the horizon across the water. That's Café Hafa, and the cafe itself is the picture.
card.stand_here: Stand right at Café Hafa, where the phone icon on the map sits. Face the sea so the tiered terraces fill the foreground and the Strait of Gibraltar and the Spanish coast sit behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the terraces with the sea and horizon behind. Go to 0.5x to fit more of the stepped levels in, or try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the Spanish coast near Tarifa or details on the tables.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sea or the sky, then drag the brightness slider down a little so the water keeps its colour and the white walls don't glare.
card.best_time: Go in the afternoon, because service may not run in the morning. Late afternoon into sunset is the best window, when the light over the water is at its warmest.
card.selfie_here: Try the steps of the cafe, on the stairways between the terrace levels, which are a popular selfie spot with the local crowd. Use the front camera (or 0.5x if your phone has it) and keep the sea view behind your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The steps are uneven, with some too tall and not all the same height, so watch your footing when you pose. Please be considerate of other guests when you take photos.
card.challenge: Build a three-layer shot: a terrace table in front, the sea in the middle, and Spain on the horizon.
card.good_to_know: Café Hafa opened in 1921 and still keeps its original look. Its terraces step down in several levels towards the Strait of Gibraltar. Paul Bowles, William S. Burroughs, The Beatles and the Rolling Stones are all listed among its past visitors. The cafe is on a steep cliff with steps, so check opening times before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at Café Hafa, where the phone icon on the map sits. Face the sea so the tiered terraces fill the foreground and the Strait of Gibraltar and the Spanish coast sit behind them.

The terraces are cut into the cliff, so the sea view is the backdrop, though the page does not say exactly which step gives the best frame.

No page gave selfie stick or tripod rules, so rules is empty. The Tripadvisor review is about 1,000+ days old, and a 2026 guide says photography is generally welcomed, but it does not mention tripods. The café's coordinates given in the request were not checked against any page.

card.hook: Picture a big round square that tips downhill like a shallow bowl, with a marble fountain in the middle and people crossing it from every direction. That's the Grand Socco, and the best way to see it is from the top.
card.stand_here: Stand on La Terrasse, at the top of the steps at the highest point of the square, across from the police station. Face north-east and the middle of the square, with its fountain and palms, is right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole sloping square in. Then go to 1x for a tidier shot of the fountain and palms, and try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the Bab Al Fahs gate or the café tables.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the fountain on a crossing point with a palm on each side, then tap the fountain and drag the slider a touch darker so the sky and pale paving don't wash out.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon gives softer light and gentler shadows than midday. At dusk, use night mode and rest your phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Head to the keyhole-shaped Bab Al Fahs gate on the edge of the square, where the medina starts. Use the front camera (zoom 0.5x if yours has it) and let the gate sit over your shoulder. It's a popular postcard subject, so check the angle on the spot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across the square from the tiled Sidi Bou Abid minaret on the southern side, so the square and the minaret both fit in the frame, with you posing in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: Ask before taking close-ups of people, and give a nod or a smile first. Photos of the square, the cafés and the architecture are fine. In the busy crush, keep bags zipped and your phone in your pocket when you're not using it, because pickpocketing is the main risk.
card.challenge: Put the fountain on a gridline crossing with a palm on each side, then take a short burst and catch someone mid-stride crossing the square.
card.good_to_know: The official name is Place du 9 Avril 1947, after the speech Sultan Mohammed V gave in Tangier on that date. "Socco" comes from the Arabic word for a market, and the square still works as a meeting point, with cafés, shops and a mosque around its edge. It was redeveloped in 2005.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on La Terrasse, at the top of the steps at the highest point of the square, across from the police station. Face north-east and the middle of the square, with its fountain and palms, is right in front of you.

card.hook: Tangier has a way of handing you the whole story in one frame, and the Hotel Continental terrace is where it does it: sea, port, and tiles that look like they've been waiting for you.
card.stand_here: Head for the Hotel Continental terrace (36 Rue Dar El Baroud) in the Medina. The phone icon marks the hotel itself, so look for the terrace inside, then face out over the bay and port.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the bay and port. Switch to zoom 0.5x if the space is tight, and try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for close-ups of tile patterns and decor.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the horizon on the upper or lower line, and let a patch of mosaic sit in one corner for depth.
card.best_time: Daylight is easiest, ideally when the café is open and quiet. Soft morning or late-afternoon light flatters the tiles and water, but check the hotel's times before you go.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the hotel terrace, facing out over the bay and port, so the hotel building is behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x to fit more in, and keep a bit of the bay in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: The terrace is part of a working hotel, so check it's open and visitors are welcome before you go, and be considerate of guests and staff. Access can be slippery on wet days.
card.challenge: Take two frames: one wide shot of the bay with a corner of tiles, and one close-up of a mosaic so good your friends ask where it is.
card.good_to_know: The Hotel Continental dates from 1870 and is one of the oldest hotels in Tangier. It was founded by the Ben Dahans, an old Jewish family of the city. Its 19th-century guestbook is said to carry the names of Edgar Degas, Winston Churchill and the Beat poets, and parts of The Sheltering Sky were filmed here.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the Hotel Continental terrace (36 Rue Dar El Baroud) in the Medina. The phone icon marks the hotel itself, so look for the terrace inside, then face out over the bay and port.

card.hook: Picture café tables spilling onto the paving, shuttered facades, and a steady stream of people squeezing out of narrow lanes. That's the Petit Socco, the social heart of Tangier's old town, and it's a lot of fun to watch before you even take a photo.
card.stand_here: Stand in front of the Palais Zahia, the old State Bank building on the Petit Socco, and face across the square. Photograph from the public square, not from inside the hotel.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the square and the hotel into one frame, because this place is tight. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) to pick out shutters and café tables.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and keep the vertical lines of the buildings straight so they don't lean.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning for a calmer, emptier square. In the evening the café terraces light up and the place is at its liveliest. Night mode helps then, so lean on a wall to keep your phone steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the Gran Café Central terrace on the north side of the square, which has a view over the Petit Socco. Use the front camera and zoom 0.5x so the square sits behind your shoulder. It's not a famous selfie spot, so check how it looks on the day. You can also try a selfie in front of the Palais Zahia facade, though the square may only be partly in frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The Palais Zahia is a private hotel, so take your photos from the square. It's polite to ask permission before close-up photos of people, especially vendors.
card.challenge: Wait for a gap in the foot traffic and catch the square with just one person crossing it. Bonus points if they're carrying something interesting.
card.good_to_know: The Petit Socco's name mixes French and Spanish: petit means small, and zoco means market. The Palais Zahia was the head office of the State Bank of Morocco from 1907 to 1952, and it became a hotel in 2017. The Hotel Fuentes and the Gran Café Central, both from the early twentieth century, are still on the square.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in front of the Palais Zahia, the old State Bank building on the Petit Socco, and face across the square. Photograph from the public square, not from inside the hotel.

card.hook: Most of the medina's doors hide behind plain walls, but this one shows off. A green-and-white tiled front, a wooden canopy and a minaret in white stucco lace, all in one narrow street.
card.stand_here: Stand on Rue de la Marine, opposite the main entrance, with the public fountain close by across from the doorway. Face the mosque and look up at the façade and minaret. Stay in the street and photograph the outside only.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural look. If the façade and minaret won't both fit, tap 0.5x. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the tile and stucco detail up the tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the minaret up with a vertical line so it doesn't lean, then leave a little space above it so the top isn't cut off.
card.best_time: Go earlier in the day, when the street is usually quieter. Pick a moment when the façade is evenly lit, not half in deep shadow.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Borj el Marsa terrace right beside the mosque, reached by stepping down from the Petit Socco area. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and put the minaret and mosque walls over your shoulder with the port and Strait behind you. Check the framing on the spot, as it depends on where you stand.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Rue de la Marine facing the main façade, where the doorway and minaret both fit, while you stand in front of the entrance.
card.rules_and_safety: The mosque is in use and closed to non-Muslims, so photograph the outside only. Don't photograph worshippers without their permission, and don't take pictures during prayer times.
card.challenge: Find the horseshoe-arch fountain across from the entrance and fit a bit of its tilework in the corner of your shot, with the minaret still standing straight.
card.good_to_know: This is the main Friday mosque of the old medina. The site is believed to have held a Roman temple and later a church before becoming a mosque. Sultan Moulay Slimane had it rebuilt in 1817-18, and the doorway's patterns, green colouring and wooden canopy are largely from the early 1800s.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Rue de la Marine, opposite the main entrance, with the public fountain close by across from the doorway. Face the mosque and look up at the façade and minaret. Stay in the street and photograph the outside only.

card.hook: A church that looks like it wandered in from a Moroccan postcard? That's St Andrew's: whitewashed walls, white pillars, a bright green gate and a bell tower shaped like a minaret.
card.stand_here: Walk north-west to the church on Rue d'Angleterre, then stand on the street opposite the church gate. Face the whitewashed front with its green gate and white pillars.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole front in. If the street is too narrow, drop to 0.5x and keep the building in the middle so the edges don't stretch. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the gate, the pillars or the bell tower.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white wall, then slide the brightness down a little so the whitewash keeps its detail and the green gate stays rich.
card.best_time: Go when the sun isn't harsh on the white front, like morning or late afternoon, and check the light on the day. Skip service times, or ask first.
card.selfie_here: If the grounds are open, try the stone paths among the garden trees and benches in the churchyard, with the church behind you. Use the front camera, zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the building sit over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a working church, so be quiet and respectful, and ask before photographing anyone or anything during a service. Photos are generally fine, but don't use flash inside. Check opening times before you go. The area is generally safe, with the usual travel precautions.
card.challenge: Keep your phone perfectly level and get those white pillars standing dead straight, with a little street left at the bottom.
card.good_to_know: Hassan I of Morocco gave the land to Tangier's British community in 1880. The first small church soon proved too small, so a bigger one went up in 1894 and was consecrated in 1905. Henri Matisse painted the church in 1913 in his Landscape Viewed from a Window.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk north-west to the church on Rue d'Angleterre, then stand on the street opposite the church gate. Face the whitewashed front with its green gate and white pillars.

selfie_research.notes: No page names a selfie spot with the church in the background, and none names a passer-by vantage point showing the whole church, so ask_someone_spot is null. The garden spot is inferred from garden descriptions, not a stated photo spot. Addresses differ across pages (Rue d'Angleterre 50; Rue de la Liberté; Avenue d'Italie), and the Find a Grave cemetery GPS (35.78337, -5.81435) is about 0.7 km east of the position you gave. Pages say Matisse painted the church from a room at the Grand Hotel Villa de France across the road, but that is a hotel room, not a public spot, so I left it out. No page mentions selfie sticks or tripods.
